item.title: Characterizing the role of Nephronectin during Anterior Eye Development in Mice
item.description:
Wednesday, August 5, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Keck Hall

  Speaker: Matthew Robert Garis Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: BioSciences-Biochemistry and Cell Biology Location: Keck Hall 102 Anterior eye development is a complex process involving the migration, proliferation, patterning and interactions between many difference cell types in order to achieve the niche tissue properties required for proper sight. The periocular mesenchyme interacts with nascent ocular tissues and extracellular matrix proteins to provide a transparent cornea. While support structures like sensory nerves and anterior eye vasculature are formed and patterned with tight spatiotemporal regulation to sustain ocular structures. Cellular interactions with the extracellular matrix are essential in regulating these morphogenic processes, but which specific component proteins achieve these effects and the signaling pathways involved are not well understood. These studies were developed to further understand the role of the extracellular matrix protein nephronectin (Npnt) during anterior eye development. While the protein has been researched during avian cornea development, its role in mice was yet to be described. The method by which these two organisms develop the cornea varies greatly and this opened the potential to discover species-specific functions of Npnt. To this end, I utilized a Npnt mutant mouse model to probe how the murine cornea is formed without this matrix protein. I show that Npnt is utilized as a migration substrate by the periocular mesenchyme (POM), as its absence leads to a reduction in corneal thickness and decreased cell counts but does not affect proliferation capacity. This result was confirmed via in vitro POM explant experiments demonstrating the ability for these cells to use Npnt as a substrate to migrate upon and blocking the EGFR pathway abolished that capacity. Thus, I found Npnt to mediate the migration of POM cells into the murine cornea during development by activation of the EGFR pathway. Npnt has been shown to play a role in angiogenesis and sensory nerve patterning during development but the protein's involvement in these processes during anterior eye development has never been investigated. I show that Npnt has the correct spatiotemporal expression to potentially influence the migration and patterning of the vasculature and nerves that project to the anterior eye. Utilizing whole mount immunohistochemistry experiments, I found that Npnt is needed for the proper patterning of the choroid vasculature and for the proper projection profile of sensory nerve innervation into the anterior eye. I furthered these results using primary neuron cell culture experiments of dissociated trigeminal ganglia from embryonic mice, discovering that Npnt attenuates migration of sensory nerves in an integrin dependent manner. Finally, I definitively determined the developmental stage at which the corneal endothelial basement membrane, the Descemet's membrane (DM), is first formed with transmission electron microscopy. Npnt is expressed by the endothelial cells during development and is integrated into the membrane with changing spatial expression relative to other major basement membrane components. I found that Npnt is expressed not only during development of the membrane but is sustained throughout the life of an organism, suggesting it may be involved in the maintenance of the corneal endothelium or in the Descemet's membrane barrier functions. Overall, in this thesis, I identified a species-specific mechanism for how the extracellular matrix protein Npnt facilitates POM migration into the developing cornea. I expanded upon this by finding Npnt is a substrate for endothelial vasculature and sensory nerves during anterior eye formation. Identifying these functional roles for Npnt during development and noting its continued expression in the Descemet's membrane provides the basis for Npnt and its receptors being potential targets for corneal cell-matrix therapies.   Matthew Garis is inviting you to a scheduled Zoom meeting. item.title: Advancing Genetic Code Expansion: From Genome-Wide Host Reprogramming to Innovative Biological Applications
item.description:
Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Mengxi Zhang Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Chemistry Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 282 Genetic code expansion (GCE) enables noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) with diverse chemical and physical properties to be introduced into proteins at defined positions. This technology has provided valuable tools for protein labeling, functional regulation, biomolecular engineering and the investigation of biological processes. Despite the rapid development of GCE, many genetically encoded ncAAs have been demonstrated primarily at the level of protein incorporation, while their potential for solving broader biological and engineering problems remains underexplored. In addition, the production of ncAA-containing proteins is often limited by inefficient stop-codon suppression and by the cellular environment in which the orthogonal translation system operates. In this dissertation, we expand the applications of genetically encoded ncAAs in material engineering and live-cell imaging and investigate endogenous host factors that regulate ncAA-containing protein production. To introduce material-binding properties into proteins and living cells, 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA), a catechol-containing amino acid found in mussel adhesive proteins, was genetically incorporated into proteins at defined positions. Optimization of the DOPA incorporation system enabled the production of homogeneous DOPA-containing proteins with enhanced binding to a broad range of organic and inorganic materials. The material-binding capability of DOPA was further combined with intrinsically disordered proteins to generate adhesive antifouling proteins. Extending this strategy from proteins to living cells, DOPA was incorporated into a bacterial surface protein to substantially enhance bacterial attachment to different materials. The improved interaction between engineered bacteria and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) also facilitated bacterial degradation of PET, demonstrating the application of GCE in protein, material and cellular engineering. In addition to creating new protein functions, genetically encoded ncAAs can serve as compact probes for studying dynamic biological processes. A series of rotor-based fluorescent ncAAs was developed to monitor local protein microenvironment changes in living cells. Among these amino acids, AnapTh displayed strong responses to environmental polarity and viscosity. Computational redesign of an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enabled the site-specific incorporation of AnapTh into proteins in mammalian cells. Placement of AnapTh at selected residues allowed real-time monitoring of local environmental changes during the aggregation of human superoxide dismutase and Huntingtin proteins and during the clustering of STIM1 and CRY2. Distinct fluorescence responses observed at different incorporation sites revealed spatially resolved changes within individual protein regions, providing a method to visualize protein aggregation, clustering and their reverse processes with high spatial precision. While these studies demonstrate the functional potential of genetically encoded ncAAs, their broader utility depends on efficient and faithful ncAA-containing protein production. To investigate how the host cell contributes to this process, a genome-wide screen of the Escherichia coli Keio single-gene knockout collection was performed using a dual-fluorescent amber-suppression reporter. Nine gene deletions reproducibly altered reporter production across different ncAA incorporation systems, indicating that GCE is regulated by diverse endogenous cellular processes. Among these candidates, rplI, which encodes the 50S ribosomal protein bL9, was further investigated. Deletion of rplI reduced overall protein expression, increased relative amber-codon readthrough and decreased the translation elongation rate, linking ribosome dynamics to ncAA incorporation. Sequence Display was subsequently used to examine the sequence-function landscape of RplI and identified its C-terminal region as an informative target for further engineering. Together, this dissertation develops and explores important applications of genetically encoded ncAAs while providing insights into the host translational mechanisms that govern their incorporation.   (Department : Chemistry)

item.title: Quantifying Many-Body Contextuality with Multiplayer Nonlocal Games from Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Space Science Building

  Speaker: Wanbing Zhao Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Space Science Building 301A Quantum contextuality is a fundamental property of quantum mechanics that captures the impossibility of reproducing quantum measurement outcomes from pre-existing classical values. Contextuality in few-particle quantum systems is commonly studied using Bell inequalities, but its emergence in large-scale, many-particle quantum systems remains poorly understood. Such many-body contextuality has attracted renewed attention in quantum information science through its formulation in terms of "nonlocal games" played with stabilizer codes, which are mathematically equivalent to Bell inequalities. However, work in this field has largely focused on determining whether such nonlocal games exhibit quantum advantage. To quantify many-body contextuality, we develop a systematic theory of nonlocal games defined on n-qubit stabilizer codes via nonlinear Boolean functions. The theory yields a universal upper bound of 7/8 on the classical value of such games that admit quantum advantage. For cyclic cluster states and toric codes, we prove that the classical values of the associated games approach 1/2 exponentially fast in n, resulting in exponentially large Bell-inequality violations. Going beyond these lattice examples, we show that exponential Bell-inequality violations are generic among random graph states, occurring with high probability over Erdős–Rényi ensembles with fixed edge probability p \in (0,1). These results provide a scalable path toward testing quantum contextuality on current and future quantum devices.   (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

item.title: Thalamo-cortical evoked effective connectivity to guide personalized neuromodulation in epilepsy
item.description:
Friday, August 7, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Jasper Wang Masters Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Electrical and Computer Engineering Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 875 Thalamic deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a promising treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. Besides the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT), the only FDA-approved target, the centromedian nucleus (CM) and pulvinar have also been shown to be promising targets. However, outcomes vary both across and within stimulation targets, and to date there is no consensus on the optimal stimulation site within each thalamic nucleus. Here, we hypothesized that effective connectivity, as quantified by thalamo-cortical evoked potentials (TCEPs), could guide personalized DBS target selection. We recorded scalp EEG responses to single-pulse electrical stimulation delivered via thalamic DBS electrodes in 15 epilepsy patients. Voxel-based linear mixed-effects modeling was applied to TCEP data to generate stimulation-response maps with high spatiotemporal resolution. We provided group-level TCEP stimulation-response maps of the CM and pulvinar, and showed that pulvinar and CM subregions selectively engage distinct cortical networks, detectable with non-invasive scalp EEG. The pulvinar showed a medial-to-lateral gradient: medial pulvinar mapped to anterior temporal cortex, middle pulvinar to mid-temporal cortex, and lateral pulvinar to parietal and posterior temporal cortex. Lateral-dorsal CM showed strong connectivity to frontocentral regions. Finally, we demonstrated a significant correlation between acute TCEP response and long-term seizure reduction rate within the same patient cohort, supporting the clinical translational potential of this approach.   Zoom link: https://www.google.com/url?q=https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/93695667394?pwd%3DBlRXICqUVKI2MZvD1W2ySZwFarWfq1.1&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1785182094516539&usg=AOvVaw321gy5b1gZlvJrgy-BIX9J (Department : Electrical and Computer Engineering)

item.title: Intoxication in British Literature, 1660-1760
item.description:
Monday, August 10, 2026 at 4 PM

  Speaker: Rowan Morar Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: English "Intoxication in British Literature, 1660-1760" argues for reading literary representations of intoxicants and altered states of mind, as a normative condition of Enlightenment life and a feature of literary representation itself. Drawing from social history, I trace how mass markets for drugs, such as plantation produced tobacco and spirits, as well as opium left their imprints on the works of key authors of British literary history—Lord Rochester, Aphra Behn, Daniel Defoe, and Charlotte Lennox. I argue that these writers from 1660-1760, the Restoration to the mid-Enlightenment period, represented the influx of colonially produced drugs that became fiscal necessities for statecraft in order to make tacit assumptions about everyday self-regulation, socialization, and politics visible. Profane appetites were as fundamentally changed in Britain as they were central to concepts of subjectivity in the violent colonial theaters producing the intoxicants for an era of taste and refinement. The construction of a subjective experience of intoxication in poems, the performance of drunkenness on the stage, the narrative accounts of inner consciousness affected by rum or tobacco, wine or opium—all offer means for seeing double: the work of intoxicants on literature and literary intoxication during an increasingly global era of mass intoxication.   https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/s/92686072682 (Department : English)

item.title: An Apparatus for Quantum Simulation with Rydberg Atoms
item.description:
Monday, August 10, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Brockman Hall for Physics

  Speaker: Brent Kruzel Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Brockman Hall for Physics 300 This thesis presents the design, construction, and characterization of a new experimental platform for quantum simulation using ultracold strontium-88 Rydberg atoms. The apparatus was developed to support future optical-tweezer based experiments that realize synthetic dimensions through coherent millimeter-wave coupling between neighboring Rydberg states while providing the optical access, electric- and magnetic-field control, and state-sensitive detection required for precision measurements. A new science chamber was designed and integrated with laser cooling, selective field ionization, and charged-particle detection systems, while electromagnetic simulations were used to optimize millimeter-wave delivery and field uniformity. Experimental characterization of the completed apparatus includes measurements of static electric-field compensation, millimeter-wave polarization purity, and coherent Rydberg spectroscopy through Rabi and Ramsey techniques. In addition, analysis methods were developed to extract relative Rydberg-state populations from selective field ionization signals, and new high-precision microwave spectroscopy measurements were incorporated into an updated determination of the quantum defect Rydberg-Ritz parameters for the singlet S, P, and D Rydberg series of strontium. Together, these developments establish the experimental and analytical foundation for future quantum simulation experiments on this new apparatus.   (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

item.title: Essays on the Energy Transition in Electricity Markets
item.description:
Wednesday, August 12, 2026 at 9 PM

Location: Baker Hall

Renewable energy is restructuring the generation mix in electricity markets, simultaneously driving thermal retirement, substantially suppressing wholesale energy prices when and where they are generating, and redirecting investment toward new technologies such as battery storage to compensate for their effects. This dissertation studies all three channels in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market. Each chapter takes a different angle and methodology: structural estimation of retirement decisions, analytical equilibrium theory for renewable dynamics, and reduced-form spatial analysis of investment composition. The first chapter estimates a dynamic discrete choice model of retirement for natural gas and coal-fired generators in ERCOT, treating exit as an irreversible optimal stopping problem under forward-looking expectations. All 45 observed exits in the estimation panel occur at strictly positive operating profit, consistent with retirement as a forward-looking continuation-value decision rather than a current-period margin trigger. The retirement decision in the model has two channels: a current-period flow payoff in which operating profit and age enter directly, and a forward-looking continuation value that summarizes the expected path of future operating profit. Operating profit is constructed at unit resolution from a 15-minute spark-spread payoff that combines real-time nodal locational marginal prices (LMPs) and fuel-cost indices (Henry Hub for gas units, delivered coal costs for coal units). Ancillary service revenue recovered from the ERCOT 60-Day Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED) record is added, and pro-rated fixed operating and maintenance costs are subtracted. Operating profit enters the flow payoff positively and significantly (coefficient +0.653, t-statistic 3.15 under a random-effects specification). Generator age enters negatively (-0.510), marginal under random effects and strongly significant without them. Wind and solar shape retirement decisions through the operating-profit transition kernel rather than the flow payoff. Their persistence in the kernel transmits into continuation values, which is how the model captures the effect of renewable trajectories on exit. Both kernel coefficients are negative (wind -0.157, solar -0.030), reflecting the merit-order erosion of incumbent operating profit, with wind the stronger channel and solar the weaker. Two counterfactual exercises explore the implications of the estimated structural model. A wind-versus-solar dose-response varies zonal renewable shares and shows how marginal renewable expansion reshapes the composition of the surviving fleet. A forward projection built from the April 2026 ERCOT Generator Interconnection Status report calibrates expected renewable buildout. Through 2035, the fleet's existing age distribution dominates retirement, while the renewable buildout contributes only marginally. The structural estimates and counterfactuals provide a reference point for policymakers and market planners assessing how the dispatchable thermal fleet evolves under continued renewable buildout in ERCOT. The second chapter extends the analytical framework of Green and Leautier (2015) in two directions. First, we derive a complete set of marginal impact results under a Feed-in Premium (FiP), an extension they identified as an open problem. Under FiP, renewable producers receive the wholesale price plus a fixed premium per MWh and curtail output when the price falls below the negative of the premium. The results cover the long-run generation mix, the per-MW market value of renewables, the equilibrium tax, and the required marginal subsidy. Because renewables avoid producing in the worst-priced states, the per-MW market value of renewable capacity falls more slowly as renewable penetration grows under FiP than under a fixed-price Feed-in Tariff. Second, we adapt the framework to the ERCOT market, which uses an Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) to set scarcity prices in lieu of a forward capacity market. ERCOT's ORDC applies a scarcity adder to the real-time energy price when operating reserves are low, calibrated to the expected cost of the curtailment those reserves would prevent. Throughout the chapter's sample period (2019-2023), the ORDC operated as an ex post adder to the energy clearing price under sequential energy and ancillary service auctions, rather than as a co-optimized shadow value within a single security-constrained dispatch. We adopt the economic logic of Hogan (2013), who derived the ORDC for a co-optimized setting, and adapt it to this pre-co-optimization institutional environment. The principal theoretical result is that the ORDC does not directly affect the rate at which renewable per-MW values fall with renewable penetration. Where infra-marginal conventional generators are at capacity, marginal changes in reserves shift rents to those generators without altering the rate at which renewable value declines. The ORDC's effect on renewable values therefore operates indirectly, through the equilibrium generation mix. A calibration exercise using ERCOT data confirms three qualitative findings. The FiP reduces the per-MW subsidy needed to sustain renewable entry and slows the rate at which the per-MW value of renewables falls. Nuclear capacity exits the equilibrium at approximately 80 GW of wind under FiT and at approximately 77 GW under ERCOT's ORDC-based market structure, while the FiP retains nuclear across the full simulated range. The earlier exit reflects a demand-channel asymmetry that the chapter establishes analytically and the calibration confirms. The combined FiP-ERCOT case is the policy-relevant one for ERCOT, since the federal Production Tax Credit shares the FiP's premium-on-top-of-price structure. Under this regime, the calibration shows substantially slower per-MW value decline than without the FiP, with nuclear retention preventing the abrupt acceleration that follows nuclear exit. This analysis bridges the analytical framework of Green and Leautier (2015) with the scarcity-pricing logic of Hogan (2013), and the ERCOT calibration provides its empirical interpretation. The third chapter estimates a discrete choice model of generator investment across ERCOT's four load zones over 2011-2024. Developers choose among five technologies (wind, solar, combined-cycle gas, open-cycle gas, and battery storage), grouped into dispatchable and non-dispatchable segments. Entry composition is estimated with a multinomial logit in the Berry (1994) log-odds inversion, with operating profit instrumented by national fuel-cost shifters and rival characteristics. Fixed cost deters entry (-3.63, p < 0.001) and federal subsidies shift composition toward the subsidized technologies (+2.29, p < 0.001). Both results are stable when year and zone fixed effects are added and when the model is re-estimated as a Poisson count model, which retains the zone-years with no entry that the log-odds inversion must drop. Entry shows no detectable response to annual energy margins. Gas-fired entry falls well below what observed payoffs alone would predict. The results quantify the mapping from ERCOT's price signals to the technology composition of investment and inform the resource adequacy debate.

item.title: Physics-informed machine learning for reconstructing dark matter and neutrino signals in TPCs
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 3 PM

Location: Herman Brown Hall

  Speaker: Ivy Li Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Herman Brown Hall HBH 227 Dual-phase xenon time projection chamber (TPC) experiments such as XENONnT are sensitive probes of dark matter and neutrinos, but as these detectors grow more complex and data-intensive, distinguishing signals of interest from backgrounds depends on improved data handling and novel analysis techniques. This thesis introduces multiple machine learning applications toward position and energy reconstruction for these detectors. Initial studies of semi-supervised autoencoders with partially interpretable latent spaces and recurrent neural networks for correcting ionization signal waveforms demonstrated their limitations from the lack of physics constraints. Continuous normalizing flow models were developed to learn the electric field inside TPCs with physics-motivated constraints built into their architecture. With a learned electric field, the flow model is able to correct for field distortions in position reconstruction. Compared to traditional methods, the flow model reduces calibration data requirements by 50 times, its physics-informed architecture ensures that the learned electric field is curl-free, and the improvement in position reconstruction consequently improves charge yield estimation across the energy range of interest for both WIMP and neutrinoless double beta decay searches. Finally, the thesis presents a demonstration of the flow's applications towards a probabilistic fiducial volume in next-generation experiments.   Zoom: https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/93454420074?pwd=0ePCCADW4tBbylIlayywSkxCBMyTgp.1 (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

item.title: Illuminating the dynamics of magmatic systems: from bubbles to the lithosphere, from a computer to the lab
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories

  Speaker: Gaetano Ferrante Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories KWGL 123 Volcanoes are the surface manifestation of Earth's great geodynamic forces. They provide an invaluable window into geologic processes that are hidden from direct observation, yet they represent a significant hazard for millions of people around the world. Investigating the dynamics of volcanic systems is thus crucial to better understand our planet and improve assessments of volcanic hazard. Volcanic processes occur over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, motivating the use of correspondingly diverse methodologies to investigate their dynamics. In this thesis, I will employ experiments, numerical modeling and data analysis to address some of the most fundamental, yet widely disputed, questions in volcanology. One of the major controls on the eruptive style and ensuing hazard of a volcano is the viscosity of its magma. Among other factors, gas bubbles suspended in the magma can either increase or decrease its viscosity, strongly influencing eruptive dynamics. In Chapter 1, I will present results from rheology experiments conducted on natural pumice samples to understand how bubbles affect the viscosity of magma. I will propose a new and unambiguous constitutive equation for the viscosity of bubbly magmas that can be used to better model volcanic eruptions and lava flows. Magmatic systems can extend for tens of kilometers from the asthenosphere, where magma is produced, to the Earth's surface, where it is eventually erupted. Whether volcanoes are controlled from the bottom-up or from the top-down is still a major question in volcanology. In Chapter 2, I will couple a numerical model of magma flow at the lithospheric scale with surface-available observations collected during the past 30 years at Kīlauea volcano (Hawaiʻi), to shed light on the dynamics of its magmatic supply pathway. "Why do eruptions end?" is a fundamental, yet overlooked question in volcanology. In 2018, Kīlauea experienced its largest eruption in more than 200 years of history, providing an unprecedented set of observations that helped volcanologists improve our understanding of caldera-forming eruptions. More than 8 years after the start of the eruption, the reasons underlying its sudden and unexpected conclusion still remain, for the most part, a mystery. In Chapter 3, I will jointly analyze a diverse set of geophysical data collected during Kīlauea's 2018 eruption to shed light on its progression and enigmatic end, providing a framework to interpret the evolution of past and future caldera-forming eruptions.   https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/4149242694?pwd=YWZsUDhEVWthT3E3R041SkpNMk5uQT09&omn=99605727293 (Department : Earth, Environmental and Planetary Sciences)

item.title: Bayesian Inference and Medical AI: From Period Estimation to Cardiac Volume Prediction
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 8 PM

  Speaker: Tony Gao Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Statistics This thesis presents three projects unified by their focus on developing and applying statistical and machine learning methods for robust parameter estimation across different scientific domains. In the first project, the accurate estimation of the periodicity of variable stars is important for understanding their physical properties and behaviors. While current methods may give accurate point estimates, uncertainty quantification is often missing. We develop a fast semi-parametric Bayesian model for period estimation that provides principled uncertainty quantification. We establish asymptotic consistency of the period estimator and apply the method to variable stars from the OGLE II project. The subsequent two projects focus on automating diagnosis in medical imaging with Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Emerging AI models provide accurate left ventricular volume estimates from echocardiograms (echo) compared to human experts when echo is used as the reference. However, a combination of poor image quality, human error, and volume assumptions of echo may not provide accurate estimation. We therefore use cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) estimates as the reference standard because they are more accurate and reproducible. We apply and assess two state-of-the-art foundational models in a novel Houston Methodist cohort in which patients underwent both echo and CMR within 24 hours of each other. Finally, we develop a custom AI model fine-tuned on these data, which substantially improves upon the off-the-shelf models and performs comparably to human experts. https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/93352464646?pwd=qDte6U4fVL4UU90ACeCbLyhiz8vxgj.1   (Department : Statistics)

item.title: Binder Jetting Process Optimization: Predicting Powder Spreading Via Rheology and Enhancing Jetting Performance through Machine Learning
item.description:
Friday, August 14, 2026 at 2 PM

Location: Mechanical Engineering Building

  Speaker: Wesley Combs Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Mechanical Engineering Location: Mechanical Engineering Building 128 Binder jet 3D printing (BJ3DP) is a prominent powder-based additive manufacturing (PBAM) technique responsible for the production of high-performance parts in multiple industries including the aerospace, automotive, medical, tooling, and weapons fields. Low-density green parts are constructed by an iterative approach involving the spreading of powder into smooth layers and the subsequent deposition of binder droplets to form solid cross-sectional regions. A high-temperature densification process known as sintering is typically conducted to yield high-density end-use parts. Prior to sintering, powder flow in both the dry spreading and wet jetting systems is highly influential to green part dimensional accuracy, surface roughness, and mechanical properties. Furthermore, high-quality green parts tend to produce good end-use parts. The efficiency of BJ3DP can be increased through a variety of means, including qualification testing and analysis software. Powder flowability is often tested prior to printing to inform material selection and powder design, especially when dealing with previously unqualified materials, particle size distributions (PSDs), and powder treatment methods. Additionally, many machine learning (ML) tools have been developed for real-time powder bed inspection as well as part quality prediction. However, the majority of existing analysis in these two realms is specifically tailored to powder bed fusion, the other major PBAM technique.   A collection of BJ3DP powder flow analyses and jetting phase ML models are presented herein with various direct applications. First, an extensive study of powder rheology and additive manufacturing suitability is conducted on extraterrestrial regolith simulants. Space travel and colonization efforts are supported by mass hopper flow design according to Jenike Stress Theory and landing site suggestions informed by in situ resource utilization PBAM. Three Ti64 alloy powders commonly used in BJ3DP received additive manufacturing suitability factors (AMS) only 26-46% better than coarse lunar highland simulant (LHS-1) and only 33-51% better than Martian simulant with high sulfate concentration (MGS-1S). This increases confidence in using actual regolith as AM feedstock material and helps inform which types of lunar and Martian soil might perform best. Next, a similar experimental study is completed with a fully-recycled nickel superalloy called M247 and three conventionally-sourced steel powders (2205, 316, and 17-4). The feasibility of powder reclamation is supported by the relatively exceptional flow characteristics of M247, which outperforms the steel powders in terms of AMS by around 20%. A review of correlations between powder properties and flow parameters in metal powders shows that this was largely due to the high density and adequate particle size of M247. This demonstrates that the significant reduction in material cost provided by re-atomization does not necessitate a loss in powder spreadability. Moving on to the ML models, a set of multilayer perceptrons are trained to use PSD parameters to predict jetting-induced particle motion and saturation. High accuracy was exhibited by the model as it received low testing dataset mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) between 5.9% and 16.7% for the four predicted macro-parameters. These values are considerably lower than the threshold value of 25%, which was based on the variation of true output data between powder beds with nearly identical PSDs. Models are designed to reduce heuristic printing and are trained on simulations executed with an in-house computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method framework. The models can be used to determine an important user-defined jetting parameter for binder jetting printers. They can also be used to identify an optimal PSD that minimizes green part porosity and dimensional error caused by particle displacement and terminal speed. The remaining ML model developed in this thesis is a physics-informed long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network that forecasts BJ3DP ejection volume, speed, and height. The LSTM model conducts direct multi-step forecasting over a 1 millisecond horizon based on printing process parameters and recent particle ejection history. The model's predictions yielded a testing dataset $R^2 > 0.9$ and low MAPE values of 24%, 14.8%, and 2.08% for average ejection volume, speed, and height. These error values were significantly less than the following MAPE values found for 63 pairs of time series with identical printing process parameters: 99% (volume), 58% (speed), and 15% (height). In the future, the model could be deployed to assist real-time monitoring by providing rapid printing process parameter modification to improve part quality. The model could also identify anomalous printing more quickly than manual human intervention, reducing unnecessary printing waste. Collectively, powder rheology and machine learning are leveraged to provide useful information and helpful analysis tools to improve BJ3DP within ISRU efforts, powder reclamation cycles, and day-to-day industrial printing. https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/95736070182?pwd=d3HLaWwkyjyJgxIPlb707zKek120rb.1 (Department : Mechanical Engineering)

item.title: Parallel Algorithms for Performance Analysis at Exascale
item.description:
Monday, August 17, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Duncan Hall

  Speaker: Jonathon Anderson Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Computer Science Location: Duncan Hall 3012 Performance analysis is critical for the development of high-performance computing (HPC) applications targeting exascale supercomputers. State-of-the-art performance tools are unprepared to handle the complex and large application binaries, unprecedented performance data volume, and widespread GPU accelerators on these platforms. Ultimately, current tools fail to provide detailed performance insights at the full scale of an exascale supercomputer, taking significant time or compute resources in postmortem processing, or sacrificing critical detail for responsiveness.   This dissertation addresses these issues by accelerating key algorithms for postmortem performance analysis, these are correlation-bound problems where the ample parallelism is limited by the need for "correlation" between inputs. Our parallelization approach produces efficient, dense parallelism for such problems by exploiting the reorderability between key operations in carefully chosen data representations. To handle large application binaries, we introduce a novel parallel control flow graph (CFG) construction algorithm with provable correctness and validated results. Our new implementation in Dyninst achieves parallel speedup as high as 25x, and accelerates a downstream performance analysis tool by up to 8x, producing detailed binary analysis for multi-gigabyte binaries in mere minutes. To handle massive performance data at scale, we introduce a new streaming aggregation (SA) algorithm for performance data aggregation that provides efficient, dense shared-memory parallelism, and a hybrid MPI/SA algorithm that incorporates conventional distributed-memory parallelism. The combination of SA and sparse data formats developed by others accelerates HPCToolkit's analysis of large-scale application performance by as much as 81x. Using it, we successfully analyzed the performance of a real-world exascale application on a single compute node, spending 0.012% of the application's compute budget. To handle complex heterogeneous code using GPU accelerators, we introduce a novel directed calling context graph (DCCG) representation for CPU, GPU, and hybrid CPU/GPU calling context that provides detailed performance analysis for heterogeneous codes without costly space expansion. Combined with a hash-based identifier methodology to improve parallelism, our new representation accelerates multi-node MPI/SA by as much as 2x. Much of the work described in this dissertation has been integrated into upstream projects and deployed on real-world exascale platforms, supporting the development of scientific HPC applications at exascale. item.title: Defective Futures: Disability and Eugenics in American and British Literature (1896 – 1936)
item.description:
Wednesday, August 19, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Herring Hall

  Speaker: Stacie Cruz Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: English Location: Herring Hall 255 "Defective Futures: Disability and Eugenics in American and British Literature (1896 – 1936)" interrogates the ways that novels in the late 19th to early 20th centuries utilize eugenic logic and discourse, arguing that the widely popularized concept of "defectiveness" allows us to think about the interconnecting logic behind the marginalization of particular bodyminds. To this end, I focus on the ways in which novels of the period apply and also (often at the same time) critique eugenic discourse. Utilizing the widespread use of the concept of defectiveness as a term that predates our current understandings of disability, I interrogate the shifting borders between who is or is not defective depending on who is wielding the term. Analyzing works by authors such as Virginia Woolf, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, and H.G. Wells, I analyze how novels represent their relationship to the future and how they narratively imagined and created futures where various populations do or do not exist, regardless of whether the narrative itself is critical of the project of eugenics as a whole.   Each chapter critiques supposed dichotomies such as perfection and deformity, humanness and animality, and madness and rationality. And it interrogates widely held beliefs, past and present, about what a body is, and what it should do, and what a mind is, and should do. This project centers rather than marginalizes the limit cases that most scholarly discussions of the future ignore: those whose bodies and minds require us to examine our discomfort about allowing pain, defectiveness, and bodymind suffering into the future. I suggest that the eugenic logic that inflects the novels I analyze likewise influences how we think about the future today. While many of us understandably desire the creation of more just futures, I nonetheless caution that understanding the future as a utopian place where things will be "better" than they currently are often relies on eugenic thinking that eliminates "defective" populations altogether. item.title: The role of working memory in predictive processing during sentence comprehension
item.description:
Friday, August 21, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Yu Lu Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Psychology Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 706 Language comprehension is supported not only by integrating incoming words with prior information but also by using the preceding context to predict upcoming information. Prediction is an important process that contributes to processing efficiency. However, less is known about how predictive processing relates to general cognitive resources. I addressed this issue by examining the role of verbal working memory (WM) in prediction during sentence comprehension using several methodological approaches, examining eye-movements, behavioral measures, and EEG components. Experiment 1 used the visual world paradigm to examine the relation of individual differences in semantic WM, phonological WM, visual-spatial WM, processing speed, and other verbal factors to verb-mediated anticipatory eye movements. Critically, semantic WM but none of the other individual differences measures independently predicted the anticipatory eye movement effect. Experiment 2 used a sentence-completion task to examine the role of WM in sentence-final word predictions. Sentence WM load was manipulated by including conditions with prediction-irrelevant clauses placed either before or between prediction-relevant information. Global prediction accuracy declined as information load increased and further decreased when irrelevant information was at an intervening position. Participants also became more likely to generate locally supported predictions based on adjacent context. When examining individual differences factors, semantic WM, but not phonological WM, was a significant predictor. Experiment 3 tested whether the global-to-local shift in predictions would also appear in a comprehension task without overt production demand. Participants read short and long sentence contexts followed by globally expected, locally expected, or implausible endings while EEG was recorded. Longer contexts reduced acceptance of globally expected endings and increased acceptance of locally expected endings. The N400 was graded by ending type but was not modulated by sentence length. In contrast, the late frontal positivity showed a Length x Ending interaction, suggesting that information load affected later prediction revision. Together, the findings suggested that prediction involves both a more passive and an active component, that automatic semantic activation operates alongside resource-dependent mechanisms that require maintaining and combining prior context. Semantic WM appears especially important in the active prediction process, supporting the construction and maintenance of the meaning representation from which predictions are generated. When earlier context becomes less accessible, prediction and interpretation shift toward emphasizing recent local information.   (Department : Psychology)

item.title: Current Research in EEPS: Dr. Bridger Ruyle, NYU Tandon School of Engineering
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are anthropogenic compounds that contain at least one –CF3 or –CF2– group and are known as forever chemicals because they cannot fully mineralize in the environment. Although essential for modern agriculture, medicine, refrigeration, and electronics, among other industries, PFAS contamination poses risks to human health and contributes to climate change. Most research and public attention focuses on a few PFAS. This narrow focus overlooks the many hundreds/thousands of additional PFAS known as precursors that can transform into stable, terminal products in the environment. This presentation will highlight recent field work, experimental results, data synthesis, and modeling efforts aimed at improving precursor quantification using organofluorine mass balances and environmental fate, including the importance of soil retention and transformation rates. These studies will be used to discuss the role of precursors on the severity and timescales of PFAS contamination at major point sources to the environment including firefighting training facilities, wastewater treatment facilities, and farmlands.

item.description:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 10 AM

Location: Moody Center

Across Two Seas brings together scholars, curators, artists, and community members for a multi-day symposium at Rice University on Black subjectivities across the medieval and early modern Mediterranean, Islamic world, and Indian Ocean. Through panels, film screenings, public conversations, and interdisciplinary dialogue, the symposium explores how Black subjects were represented in artistic, literary, and documentary sources and how these representations were shaped by trade, travel, religion, knowledge-making, and cultural exchange. By connecting Europe, North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa, India, and Southeast Asia, Across Two Seas expands the geography of premodern race studies and places the Indian Ocean at the center of conversations too often framed primarily through Europe. The symposium invites broader publics to consider how histories of Blackness were made across multiple regions, media, and worlds.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER   A proven leader and collaborator, Leslie Duke built her career on aligning business strategies with client needs, building business in new and existing marketplaces by driving innovation and developing next-generation leaders to advance the firm's vision and values. Safety is at the core of every decision she makes.  Her top commitment as CEO is to the safety and well-being of employee-owners, clients, partners and the communities the firm serves. Prior to her role as chair and CEO, Leslie served as regional president and general manager of the firm's South Central Region.  Leslie helped expand the firm's regional client base from an initial Houston client to over 650 local, regional and national clients in numerous marketplaces such as power utility, petrochemical, refining, manufacturing and space exploration.  Leslie's integral role in launching Burns & McDonnell's engineer-procure-construct (EPC) delivery method led to the development and successful execution of numerous multimillion-dollar projects.  During her tenure, Leslie's region delivered over $4 billion in revenue for environmental, consulting, engineering, procurement and construction services. Leslie joined Burns & McDonnell in 1999 as a structural engineer and advanced through a series of leadership roles, including opening offices in Austin, Dallas and Fort Worth, Texas and Raleigh, North Carolina where she served as general manager.  She became a senior vice president in 2014 and, in 2016, was named the firm's first female president. Leslie earned a bachelor's degree in civil/structural engineering from Texas Tech University and was named a Texas Tech Distinguished Engineer in 2018.  She is an emeritus member of the Dean's Council for the university's School of Engineering. Leslie and her husband, Travis, have two children.
